title: The Product Designer's new edge might be knowing how to talk to code
description: Figma is not the product. Why being able to talk to code has become an edge for Product Designers, and where design systems and AI come in.

related.title: Clint Scale
related.body: In practice: an explorable design system, with tokens, components, contrast and governance.

blocks.text: For a long time, there was a pretty clear line between design and development.
The designer thought about the experience and created the interfaces.
The developer turned that into code.
That model still exists, of course. But the way digital products get built is changing.

data.lead: With new tools, AI and processes that bring design and development closer every day, I believe there's one skill that may become more and more important for Product Designers:
data.phrase: knowing how to talk to code.

blocks.text: And I'm not saying every designer needs to become a developer.
I'm talking about understanding better how the things we design actually work.
Figma is not the product
This may sound obvious, but it's easy to forget.
A beautiful screen in Figma is just a representation of something that has to work in the real world.
When we create a component, it has to exist in code.
When we define a spacing value, it has to make sense inside the system.
When we create an interaction, it has to be technically possible.
When we think about responsiveness, we need to consider different screen sizes.
And when we create an experience, we need to understand what happens behind it.
That's why the closer the designer is to these conversations, the better the result tends to be.
We don't need to know how to code everything
I think this distinction matters.
A Product Designer doesn't need to be able to build a complete product alone.
You don't need to master React, Node, databases, APIs and every technology the team uses.
But understanding a few concepts can change the way you work quite a bit.

questions: What does a responsive interface mean?
How can a variable change an interface?
What happens when a request takes too long?
How does a form behave when there's an error?
close: These questions are part of the user experience.
And understanding a bit of the technology helps the designer think about these situations before they turn into problems.

blocks.text: Design and code are getting closer
Tools like Figma Make and other AI-based solutions are making it easier to turn ideas into working prototypes and code.

blocks.caption: The path between design and what reaches the user got shorter.

blocks.text: That shifts the dynamic a bit.
Before, we could create an interface in Figma and wait for development to find out how that idea would really work.
Now we can try out some of those ideas much faster.
That doesn't mean the designer will replace the developer.
The way I see it, it's exactly the opposite.
The trend is more collaboration between the two.
The designer understands the technical possibilities better.
The developer gets to join experience decisions earlier.
And the product can be built with less distance between what was imagined and what actually ships.
Knowing code also helps you ask better questions
This may be one of the biggest benefits.
Imagine you designed an interaction and the developer says:
“That's going to be hard to build.”
Without technical knowledge, it's easy to just accept it or insist on the original solution.
But when you understand a little more about development, the conversation can change:

items: “Is there another way to do it?”

blocks.text: “If we do it this way, can we keep the same goal?”

data.d: What's the best solution for the product?

blocks.text: That's way more productive.
Code can also help the design process
For a long time, we thought of code as something that happens after design.
But maybe that separation is becoming less relevant.
We can use code to:

items: build prototypes closer to the real product;
create experiences that would be hard to represent in a design tool alone.

blocks.text: That expands the designer's ability to experiment.
And the cheaper it gets to experiment, the more ideas we can test.
Design systems also bring the two worlds together
A good design system is a great example of this connection.
In Figma, we have components, variants, styles and tokens.
In code, we have reusable components, properties, states and rules.
If the two sides don't talk, problems start.
The Figma component doesn't represent the real component.
The developer has to interpret decisions that should already be clear.
When design and code are closer, the design system stops being just a visual library.
It becomes a shared language between design and development.

blocks.caption: When Figma and code use the same tokens, the design system becomes a shared language.

blocks.text: So where does AI come in?
AI is making this conversation even more interesting.
Today we can already ask a tool to generate an interface, turn an idea into code, create variations or even explore different solutions.
That speeds things up a lot.
But speed doesn't necessarily mean quality.
If I can generate 20 interfaces in a few minutes, I still need to know:
Which one solves the problem best?
Which one is accessible?
Which one is technically feasible?
Which one is simpler?
Which one fits with the rest of the product?
Which one actually improves the experience?
AI can help produce.
But someone still has to make the decisions.
And that's still one of the designer's main roles.
The edge may be in the connection
Maybe the Product Designer of the future isn't the designer who knows the most tools.

blocks.caption: It's not about knowing how to code everything; it's about understanding the product's material.

blocks.text: Nor necessarily the one who codes best.
It may be the one who moves best between different areas.
And being able to talk with different professionals without having to speak the same technical language they do.
In the end, we don't need to turn Product Designers into developers.
But I believe we need to grow designers who better understand what happens after the Figma file is handed off.

data.a: Because the work doesn't end when the interface is ready.
data.b: That's when it starts to really exist.
